what_it_is.prose: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) is a Maharatna Category-I Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Defence, Government of India, headquartered at 15/1, Cubbon Road, Bengaluru. Founded in 1963 (with roots back to 1940 as Hindustan Aircraft), HAL is India's flagship aerospace OEM and the prime contractor for the LCA Tejas fighter programme, the Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter, the Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) Prachand, and the Sukhoi Su-30MKI license-build programme. As of 31 March 2026, HAL's order book stood at ₹2,54,538 crore — the largest in the company's history and approximately 7-8 years of revenue visibility, up from ₹1,89,000 crore at the start of FY26. The order book includes 180 LCA Tejas Mk-1A (ordered March 2026 for ₹62,370 crore), 156 LCH Prachand, 34 Dhruv ALH, and 97 LCA Tejas Mk-1A (ordered September 2025 for ₹62,370 crore). For FY26, HAL reported standalone revenue from operations of ₹33,050 crore (up 7% YoY from ₹30,981 crore in FY25) and EBITDA of ₹13,472 crore (approximately 30% margin, up 11% YoY). Q1 FY27 results showed continued momentum with revenue of ₹5,533 crore (up 25.3% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,048.33 crore (up 8.2% YoY). HAL's export revenue for FY26 was ₹501 crore (up from ₹400 crore in FY25), driven by Do-228 deliveries to Guyana and Mauritius. The single most critical programme risk is the GE Aerospace F404-IN20 engine supply chain for the Tejas Mk-1A: only 6 of 99 engines contracted in August 2021 had been delivered as of April 2026, with the chokepoint traced to a South Korean firm with financial issues. HAL has levied liquidated damages on GE Aerospace and an in-country F404 depot is being established with GE (announced April 2026). The Tejas Mk-2 will use the GE F414-INS6 engine, which saw a reported 3x price hike in June 2026, with Transfer of Technology for indigenous production not yet agreed.

faq.question: What is HAL's order book and why is the F404 engine a critical chokepoint?
faq.answer: HAL's order book stood at ₹2,54,538 crore as of 31 March 2026 — the largest in the company's history and 7-8 years of revenue visibility. The order book includes 180 LCA Tejas Mk-1A (₹62,370 cr March 2026), 156 LCH Prachand, 34 Dhruv ALH, and 97 LCA Tejas Mk-1A (₹62,370 cr September 2025). However, the Tejas Mk-1A programme is constrained by GE Aerospace F404-IN20 engine supply: only 6 of 99 engines contracted in August 2021 had been delivered by April 2026, with the chokepoint traced to a South Korean firm with financial issues. HAL has levied liquidated damages on GE Aerospace and an in-country F404 depot is being established with GE (announced April 2026).

faq.question: What is the F414 'price hike trap' for Tejas Mk-2 and AMCA?
faq.answer: The Tejas Mk-2 and AMCA Mk-1 will use the GE F414-INS6 engine (more powerful than the F404). In June 2026, Air Power Asia reported a 3x price hike on the F414, with Transfer of Technology for indigenous production not yet agreed between GE Aerospace and the Indian government. This creates a strategic risk: India's two flagship indigenous fighter programmes (Tejas Mk-2 and AMCA) will depend on a US-sourced engine with no clear path to sovereign production. The Kaveri engine programme (GTRE) has not yet produced a viable alternative.

faq.question: What is HAL's role in the AMCA 5th-generation fighter programme?
faq.answer: HAL is the production partner for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), India's indigenous 5th-generation fighter programme led by the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) and DRDO. Phase-1 of the AMCA programme has been sanctioned for ₹15,000 crore, with first flight expected in 2028-29. The AMCA Mk-1 will use twin GE F414-INS6 engines (USA), the same engine planned for the Tejas Mk-2. HAL will be the final integrator, with private-sector airframe suppliers expected to participate.
